title: How To Handle Misbehavior With Your Substitute https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2015/05/16/how-to-handle-misbehavior-with-your-substitute/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Michael Linsin offers two concrete strategies for teachers dealing with a bad behavior report from a substitute teacher. First, teachers should insist substitutes use the regular classroom management plan rather than leaving discipline to the sub's own devices, and should personally brief the substitute on expectations and follow-through, especially the first time they cover the class. Second, teachers should personally handle the class's third-level consequence—such as sending a letter home—even though a sub was present when the misbehavior occurred, so students understand that the teacher's authority and expectations remain in force even in their absence. Linsin frames the whole issue as fundamentally about the teacher's ongoing influence rather than about the substitute, the class composition, or timing.
points: A bad substitute report can be hard to address because the regular teacher wasn't present to witness the misbehavior firsthand.
Strategy one: insist substitutes use the classroom's existing management plan, and personally brief them on expectations, especially for their first time covering the class.
Strategy two: the classroom teacher should personally handle the third-level consequence (e.g., a letter home) even when a substitute was present for the misbehavior.
These steps signal to students that behavioral expectations remain unchanged in the teacher's absence, preserving the teacher's influence even 'from afar.'
Linsin frames the core issue as being about maintaining influence and consistent presence, not about the substitute, the students, or external circumstances.
quotes: Getting a bad report from your substitute can be especially frustrating. You weren’t there. You didn’t witness the misbehavior.
A common complaint from substitute teachers is that few classroom teachers leave plans for handling misbehavior, that they’re often left to their own devices.
The reason this strategy is effective is because you’re able to confidently tell your students that when you’re away, nothing changes.
This sends the message that you’re still running the show. Students are quick to misbehave with a visiting teacher when they believe there is no connection to you.
Handling the third consequence effectively keeps your looming presence, expectations, and influence active within the hearts and minds of your students.
It’s about the power of influence. It’s about maintaining an eyeball-to-eyeball connection to your class even from afar.
